hook: Push a heavy couch and at first nothing happens; push harder and it suddenly lurches forward, then slides with less effort than it took to start. Friction is not one fixed force: it adjusts while things grip and changes its rules once they slide. Telling those two cases apart is a classic place to lose points.

chain.cause: Two surfaces press together with a normal force F_N
chain.effect: they can exert friction on each other along the surface

chain.cause: The surfaces do not slide but something tries to slide them
chain.effect: static friction takes whatever value prevents slipping, up to μ_s F_N

chain.cause: The needed friction would exceed μ_s F_N
chain.effect: the surfaces slip and friction drops to kinetic friction, μ_k F_N, opposing the sliding

chain.cause: The normal force changes (a ramp, a tilted pull, a load)
chain.effect: both the maximum static friction and the kinetic friction change in proportion

ideas: Kinetic friction (sliding): fk = μkFN, opposing the sliding of the surfaces; independent of contact area and speed.
Static friction (gripping): fs ≤ μsFN. It equals whatever prevents slipping; it reaches μsFN only at the point of slipping.
Usually μ<sub>s</sub> > μ<sub>k</sub>, so a stuck object lurches once it breaks free.
Find F<sub>N</sub> from the perpendicular direction first: on a ramp it is mg cos θ, not mg. The equations sheet writes |F<sub>f</sub>| ≤ |μF<sub>N</sub>|.

misconception.wrong: Static friction on a resting object is always μ_s F_N.
misconception.right: Static friction is only as large as it needs to be. A crate pushed with 60 N that does not move has 60 N of friction, even if μ_s F_N is 206 N.

summary: Friction acts along a surface. Kinetic friction, while sliding, is μ_k F_N and opposes the sliding; static friction, while gripping, is whatever prevents slipping, up to μ_s F_N. Usually μ_s > μ_k. Find the normal force first, since it is mg cos θ on a ramp and changes with tilted pulls.
